compounding_issues: Session 4 committed binary artifacts into git (__pycache__/*.pyc and todos.db), a repo-hygiene regression that persisted through the final commit
Session 3 wires notifications using g.user['username'] where the task signature expects user_email, but the schema has no email column — a semantic mismatch baked in that no later session corrected
Session 2 hand-rolled the HS256 JWT (manual base64/hmac, no iat) and never upgraded to a library; it works and is tested, but remains security-relevant hand-rolled crypto

Session 5's cursor pagination silently changed list ordering from created_at DESC to id DESC, replacing a behavior the S1 test suite had pinned (test_list_tasks_is_newest_first was dropped in S2 and never restored)
Session 5's rate_limit_key calls get_current_user() on every request, adding a DB lookup inside the limiter key path
key_decisions: Session 2 introduced owner-scoped multi-tenancy: every task query filtered by owner_id with an idempotent ALTER TABLE migration — this ownership model became the spine of all later work
Session 2 chose a hand-rolled HS256 JWT + Werkzeug password hashing instead of adding a JWT dependency
Session 3 adopted Celery for async notifications, gated on a status transition to 'completed'
Session 4 extracted a repository layer (BaseRepository + TaskRepository/UserRepository + initialize_database), cutting app.py by ~45 net lines and moving all raw SQL out of the routes
Session 5 layered in Flask-Limiter rate limiting and cursor-based pagination as cross-cutting concerns, keeping an in-memory fallback so Redis is not hard-required
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily with a clear arc. Session 1 fixed real seed bugs (timezone-naive dates, wrong default status, missing commit) and added the first tests. Session 2 was the largest and riskiest jump — a 208-line rewrite adding auth and multi-tenancy, but it was well-tested and its test suite grew to cover migration of old schemas. Session 3 was a small, focused, well-tested integration of Celery notifications. Session 4 was the strongest refactor: it removed net code while preserving all passing tests via the repository extraction. Session 5 added cross-cutting features with tests, reaching 18/18 passing, though it introduced minor regressions (ordering change, committed binaries, username-as-email). Overall the codebase became more modular and better tested over time, with test coverage expanding in step with each feature.
story_review.summary: A coherent, well-sequenced story that improves monotonically — from bug-fix greenfield to a layered, tested, auth'd, paginated and rate-limited API — marred only by minor hygiene and semantic mismatches that never got cleaned up.
